query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the transition in dynamic behavior across different strain rates and temperatures arises from a competition between time‐dependent solute/dislocation interactions (i.e., dynamic strain aging that causes serrated flow at moderate strain rates and intermediate temperatures) and a phonon‐drag–controlled dislocation mobility regime that becomes dominant at very high strain rates. The removal of Co slightly alters the solute distribution and lattice distortions so that under dynamic loading the reduced effectiveness of solute pinning favors a sharper onset of phonon drag at a threshold dislocation velocity.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, single-phase FCC solid solution of Co‐free FeNiCrMn, with a similar grain structure and random solute distribution as the parent equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
generation.intervention: Systematic dynamic mechanical testing (e.g., using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar) over a wide range of strain rates (from ~10^−3 s^−1 to >10^3 s^−1) at several controlled temperatures (from cryogenic to near intermediate service temperatures) to probe the yield strength and flow serration characteristics.
generation.conditions: Quasi-isothermal tests in the solid-solution regime where no dynamic recrystallization or phase transformation is activated (temperatures below the onset of DRX and sufficiently below melting), comparing low (quasi-static) to high strain rate deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of dislocations interacting with local solute atmospheres versus the lattice vibrations (phonons) that impart viscous drag; the minute changes in local ordering or lattice distortion due to the absence of Co also mediate these interactions.
generation.mechanism: At moderate strain rates, dislocations have time to interact with solute atoms and form transient Cottrell atmospheres, leading to dynamic strain aging (manifest as serrations in the stress-strain curve). At high strain rates the available time is too short for these interactions, while the rapid dislocation motion increases interaction with phonons. This phonon drag effect strongly hinders dislocation motion, leading to a marked increase in flow stress. The balance between these two mechanisms changes with temperature: at lower temperatures, reduced thermal activation exacerbates solute pinning and delays dislocation release, whereas at elevated temperatures the phonon drag effect is more pronounced due to increased vibrational activity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the quasi-static baseline where serration amplitudes are modest and yield strength shows moderate rate sensitivity, tests at high strain rates should reveal (a) a significant jump in yield strength following a scaling consistent with phonon drag models and (b) a change in serration morphology – with larger or more irregular stress drops at intermediate rates that fade as the phonon drag regime takes over.
generation.baseline: Quasi-static or low strain rate deformation conditions (10^−3 s^−1) at room temperature or moderately low temperatures, where the dynamic strain aging mechanism dominates and yield strength is lower.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the deformation regime where the FCC solid solution remains stable (i.e., below the temperatures that would induce dynamic recrystallization or phase transformation) and for strain rates spanning from the quasi-static regime up to beyond 10^3 s^−1. Deviations outside these boundaries (e.g., extreme high temperatures triggering recovery or recrystallization) are not considered.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates mechanisms observed in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (as evidenced in PMC7512474 sections 1, 4.1, and 4.2) to the Co‐free derivative. It is uncertain exactly how the removal of Co quantitatively modifies the solute/dislocation interaction landscape, so while the direction of the rate and temperature effects is supported, the precise transition strain rate or yield stress increase remains approximate.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of split-Hopkinson pressure bar tests on as-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn samples at several fixed temperatures (e.g., cryogenic, room temperature, and moderately high temperature), covering strain rates from 10^−3 s^−1 up to >10^3 s^−1. Simultaneously record high-resolution stress-strain data focused on both the average yield strength and serration characteristics.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress as functions of strain rate and temperature
Serration amplitude and frequency in the stress-strain curves
Dislocation density and microstructural features via post-deformation TEM or EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength does not exhibit a stronger-than-expected rate sensitivity at high strain rates (consistent with the phonon drag prediction) or if the serration characteristics do not significantly change (i.e., remain consistent with low strain rate dynamic strain aging behavior) across the tested range, then the proposed switch in the controlling mechanism from dynamic strain aging to phonon drag is not supported, falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. The Constitutive Model and Strain-Rate Sensitivity
cited_evidence.text: The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had positive activation volume at strain rates less than 1 × 10−2 s−1. However, when the specimen deformed under high strain rates (beyond 1 × 103 s−1), the deformation time was very short. There was not enough time available for thermal energy to help dislocations overcome the barriers. The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had a different deformation mechanism at dynamic loading. According to the literature [], the large jump in yield strength at high strain rates is probably due to the phonon drag effect on the motion of dislocations. The phonon drag phenomenon becomes very effective during plastic deformation at high strain rates []. A phonon is an elastic lattice vibration propagating in a crystal []. The viscous drag generating from the interaction of the dislocations has negative impacts on the deformation progress. The drag effects by the phonons can be ignored under quasi-static conditions for low dislocation velocities. However, high dislocation velocities under high strain rates would enhance the phonon drag effects greatly and lead to phonons scattering, which also hinders dislocation movement. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.2. Mechanism for the Serration Behavior
cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys present serrations on the flow stress curves during the plastic deformation, often at a normal strain rate around 1 × 10−4 s−1 or at low temperatures. Serration behavior exhibits in the stress-strain curves of the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy at 7 K, 7.5 K, and 9 K at a strain rate of 4 × 10−4 s−1 []. The Al5Cr12Fe35Mn28Ni20 high-entropy alloy exhibits typical serration behaviors at the elevated temperatures of 573 K and 673 K, with a strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1 []. Several microstructure mechanisms are proposed to explain the serration behavior, e.g., the Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect. Serration behavior was supposed to be associated with Cottrell atmosphere interaction with moving dislocations, slip bands, and dynamic strain aging. In Figure 4, it can be seen that the stress-strain curves of the as-cast NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 show no serrations, and marked serrations are present on the stress-strain curves of specimens deformed at strain rates above 900 s−1.
